title: The Great Lakes Program Both Parties Keep Funding
hook: Since 2010 the U.S. has spent over $5 billion cleaning up the Great Lakes — and it has survived Congress after Congress. The coalition behind it is a case study in building bipartisan support.
key_points: The Great Lakes Restoration Initiative has funded 8,000+ projects since 2010 with $5B+ in federal money.
A University of Michigan study found a $3+ economic return for every $1 spent.
In 2019 the Trump administration proposed a 90% funding cut, then reversed within three weeks after Michigan Republicans objected.
Support came from a broad coalition — governors, mayors, NGOs, and tribes — not one interest group alone.
Funding is spread across every congressional district in the watershed, letting members of both parties claim credit locally.
content_html: Since 2010, the Great Lakes Restoration Initiative has funneled more than $5 billion in federal money into over 8,000 projects — cleaning up toxic sites, fighting invasive species, restoring habitat — and it has kept bipartisan support through multiple administrations. In 2019, the Trump administration proposed cutting its funding by 90%; it reversed course within three weeks after Michigan Republicans explained the program's regional importance.
extra_html: Writing in The Conversation, University of Michigan's Mike Shriberg traces the initiative's roots to a 2004 executive order from President George W. Bush declaring the Great Lakes of "national significance," with the program formally launching in 2010. Its durability, he argues, comes from a few deliberate ingredients: a coalition wider than any single interest group — governors, mayors, NGOs, and tribes all pushing together — sustained economic messaging from business leaders (a University of Michigan study found a $3+ return for every $1 spent), and a funding design that reaches every congressional district in the watershed, so lawmakers from both parties can point to results back home. Surveys cited in the piece found 96% of Great Lakes-region residents see the investment as important, regardless of party.

source.name: The Conversation
authors: Mike Shriberg, Professor of Practice & Engagement, School for Environment & Sustainability; Director of the University of Michigan Water Center, University of Michigan

related.title: Environmental Governance
related.hook: How do you regulate something that ignores borders and belongs to no one? Environmental governance is the toolkit societies use to manage nature collectively.

related.title: The Politics of Climate Change
related.hook: Climate change is a global commons problem at the largest scale — which is exactly why it's so politically hard: the costs are now, local, and certain; the benefits, future and shared.

related.title: What Public Policy Is
related.hook: Passing a law is just the start. Public policy is the whole arc — from defining a problem to actually delivering a solution and seeing whether it worked.

flashcards.prompt: What has kept the Great Lakes Restoration Initiative funded across administrations of both parties?
flashcards.back_html: A broad coalition (governors, mayors, NGOs, tribes) plus a funding formula spread across every congressional district in the watershed — so members of both parties can point to local results.

flashcards.prompt: What happened when the Trump administration proposed a 90% funding cut to the initiative in 2019?

choices.text: It reversed the cut within three weeks after Michigan Republicans pushed back
The cut passed with no opposition

flashcards.explanation_html: Local Republican pushback over the program's regional importance led the administration to reverse course quickly.

flashcards.prompt: Why does spreading funding across every district in the watershed help sustain bipartisan support?

choices.text: It lets representatives of both parties claim credit for projects in their own district
It requires unanimous consent from all 50 states
It eliminates the need for any coalition of supporters

flashcards.explanation_html: When benefits are geographically distributed, more legislators have a direct local stake in defending the program.
